newsitem.title: JAPAN: Malaysia, Thailand hit out at rich nations on aid.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia, Thailand hit out at rich nations on aid.

text.p: Malaysia and Thailand joined forces on Monday to criticise rich nations, saying their decision to cut back on aid contributions showed a lack of sensitivity to the needs of poorer countries.

"It is becoming increasingly difficult to secure adequate donor funds to finance development. Donor countries are imposing conditions that betray a lack of sensitivity to the needs of developing members," Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said at the annual meeting of the Asian Development Bank.

The multilateral financial institution, which has 56 members including the United States and Japan, is holding its 30th annual meeting in this southern Japanese city. The gathering has been marked by warnings from traditional donors that they cannot continue to be generous with aid.
The ADB must recognise the difficulties of poorer countries and make a serious effort to help its members put in place policies that would attract alternative capital, Ibrahim said.
Speaking on the second day of the bank's three-day meeting, Ibrahim said certain donor countries were setting tough conditions for aid. He did not specify what the conditions were.
"We believe these new policies (conditions) will significantly increase costs and reduce accessibility to concessionary funds," Ibrahim said.
Thailand's Finance Minister Amnuay Virawan criticised donor nations for cutting back on aid and said his own country was doing all it could to help.
"Although Thailand is still a borrowing member country and currently facing macroeconomic adjustment, we realise the importance of sharing," he said.

"We are concerned with the declining proportion of contribution from the donors' resources and would like to strongly urge traditional donors to share your wealth through ADF to assist our disadvantaged members," Virawan added.
The ADF (Asian Development Fund) is the ADB's aid window for virtually interest-free loans.
The ADF was depleted last year and only after much negotiation did donors agree to replenish it to $6.3 billion.
The money would last up to 2000 and the traditional donors have said they cannot continue contributing to it.

Japan has been the ADB's biggest donor but at the opening session on Sunday, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka signalled that budgetary constraints at home may make it less generous with aid than in the past.

"Since our fiscal situation is the worst among industrial countries, fiscal reform is among our top priorities... When implementing fiscal structural reforms, however, Official Development Assistance (ODA) cannot be exempted from our effort to cut down on expenditure," Mitsuzuka said.
Thailand and Malaysia have both been borrowers but after their recent economic success they have become donors too.
The United States on Monday praised the ADB for having successfully turned aid recipients into donors.
